# Sleep Like a Pro: Your Guide to Finally Getting a Good Night's Rest

We've all been there—staring at the ceiling at 2 a.m., calculating how many hours of sleep we'll get if we fall asleep *right now*. Poor sleep doesn't just leave us groggy; it affects our mood, focus, immune system, and long-term health. The good news? Better sleep is within reach, and it starts with a few intentional habits.

## 1. Stick to a Consistent Sleep Schedule

Your body thrives on routine. Going to bed and waking up at the same time every day—even on weekends—trains your internal clock, making it easier to fall asleep and wake up naturally. It's tempting to "catch up" on sleep Saturday morning, but shifting your schedule confuses your circadian rhythm and often leaves you feeling worse. Aim for consistency within an hour, and your body will thank you.

## 2. Create a Sleep-Friendly Environment

Your bedroom should signal one thing: rest. Keep it cool (around 65°F or 18°C is ideal for most people), dark, and quiet. Blackout curtains, a white noise machine, or a fan can work wonders. And treat your bed as a sleep-only zone—working, scrolling, or binge-watching from under the covers weakens the mental association between your bed and sleep.

## 3. Watch What You Consume

That afternoon coffee might be sabotaging your night. Caffeine can linger in your system for 6–8 hours, so try to cut it off by early afternoon. Alcohol, while it may make you feel drowsy, disrupts deep sleep and often causes middle-of-the-night wake-ups. Heavy meals late at night can also interfere with rest, so opt for a light snack if you're hungry before bed.

## 4. Put Down the Phone

The blue light emitted by phones, tablets, and TVs suppresses melatonin—the hormone that tells your body it's time to sleep. Beyond the light itself, scrolling keeps your brain stimulated and engaged. Try a "digital sunset" 30–60 minutes before bed. Swap screen time for a book, gentle stretching, or journaling instead.

## 5. Build a Wind-Down Routine

Your body needs a transition period between the busyness of the day and sleep. Develop a relaxing pre-bed ritual: take a warm shower, do some light reading, practice deep breathing, or listen to calming music. Over time, this routine becomes a cue that tells your brain it's time to power down.

## 6. Move During the Day

Regular exercise is one of the most effective ways to improve sleep quality. Even a brisk 30-minute walk can make a difference. Just be mindful of timing—intense workouts too close to bedtime can be energizing and keep you awake. Morning or afternoon exercise is ideal.

## 7. Don't Force It

If you've been lying awake for more than 20 minutes, get up and do something calming in low light—read a few pages or do a quiet activity—until you feel drowsy. Lying in bed frustrated actually teaches your brain to associate your bed with stress, making sleep even harder.

## 8. Know When to Seek Help

If you've tried everything and still struggle with chronic sleep problems, talk to a doctor. Conditions like sleep apnea, insomnia, and restless leg syndrome are common and very treatable. There's no prize for suffering through it.

## The Bottom Line

Great sleep isn't about one magic trick—it's the result of small, consistent habits working together. Start with one or two changes, like setting a consistent bedtime and cutting off caffeine earlier in the day. Your energy, mood, and health will thank you. Here's to waking up refreshed!

$$S - (36 - S) = 2S - 36 \equiv 0 \pmod{11} \implies 2S \equiv 3 \pmod{11} \implies S \equiv 7 \pmod{11}$$

Since $10 \le S \le 26$, we need $S = 18$. So the odd positions must contain four digits summing to $18$ (and even positions automatically sum to $18$ too).

**Counting subsets summing to 18:** The 4-element subsets of $\{1,\dots,8\}$ summing to $18$ are:
$$\{1,2,7,8\},\ \{1,3,6,8\},\ \{1,4,5,8\},\ \{1,4,6,7\},\ \{2,3,5,8\},\ \{2,3,6,7\},\ \{2,4,5,7\},\ \{3,4,5,6\}$$

That's **8 subsets**.
